pos: n. (the Lancashire Cistercian abbey founded in 1127, second only to Fountains in wealth among English Cistercian houses)
etymology: From Old Norse Futharnes, the headland by the rump-shaped island, from futh and nes, a headland.
biblical_def: Furness Abbey stands in a sheltered valley on the Lancashire peninsula between Morecambe Bay and the Duddon, founded in 1127 by Stephen, later king, for monks of Savigny who joined the Cistercian order in 1147. It became the second richest Cistercian house in England after Fountains, holding the whole of the Furness peninsula, the iron ore of Low Furness, fisheries, granges, ferry rights over the sands and a share of the Isle of Man's church. Its abbots ran a small state, treated with the Scots who raided them in 1316, and were lords of the manor over tenants who owed them labour. It surrendered in 1537, the first great abbey to go, after its monks were implicated in the Pilgrimage of Grace. The dictionary records Furness for the arc of it. Monks who had come north under a rule of poverty ended as the chief ironmasters and landlords of a county, and the New Testament's warnings about wealth are addressed to exactly that process: they that will be rich fall into a snare, and the love of money is a root from which men have erred from the faith.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines rich as having abundant possessions; a snare as a device for catching; a lust as an eager desire; to drown as to overwhelm in water; and perdition as utter destruction.
webster_full: RICH, a. Wealthy; opulent; possessing a large portion of land, goods or money; abundant in materials.
SNARE, n. An instrument for catching animals, particularly birds, by the leg; anything by which one is entangled and brought into trouble.
LUST, n. Longing desire; eagerness to possess or enjoy; concupiscence; evil propensity.
DROWN, v.t. To overwhelm in water; to overflow; to deluge; to immerse and suffocate in water.
PERDITION, n. Entire loss or ruin; utter destruction; the utter loss of the soul or of final happiness.
corruption_summary: Lancashire Cistercian abbey of 1127, second richest of the order in England, lord of the whole Furness peninsula; surrendered in 1537.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that wealth is a danger described in Scripture as a trap rather than merely as a distraction. Paul uses the imagery of snaring and drowning: “But they that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare” (1Ti 6:9), and he names the root of the failure without naming money itself as evil, “For the love of money is the root of all evil” (1Ti 6:10).

The live temptation for an order founded on poverty is to accept endowments faithfully and end up a landlord, which is the history of nearly every Cistercian house in Britain. Solomon gives the plain instruction that a granting charter never contains: “Labour not to be rich: cease from thine own wisdom” (Pro 23:4). Christ, asked to settle an inheritance, refused the case and gave the reason: “Take heed, and beware of covetousness: for a man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth” (Luk 12:15). Furness held a peninsula and surrendered first.

pos: n. (the Yorkshire Cistercian abbey that moved four times before settling, famous for its great rose window)
etymology: From Old English býland, land near a dwelling, or from a Norse personal name with land.
biblical_def: Byland Abbey in the North York Moors is the record holder among English monasteries for being unable to settle. Its community, Savigniac and then Cistercian, was founded in 1134 at Calder in Cumberland, driven out by the Scots, refused at Furness, sheltered at Hood, moved to Old Byland, found itself so close to Rievaulx that the two houses' bells confused each other's offices, moved again to Stocking, and finally built at Byland from 1177, forty-three years and five sites after it began. The church it then put up had a rose window twenty-six feet across in its west front, half of which still stands, and a tiled pavement that survives. It was dissolved in 1538. The dictionary records Byland for the forty-three years. A community that owned nothing settled for nothing and kept moving, and the apostolic teaching on contentment was written for exactly that condition: having food and raiment, be content; and Paul says he learned contentment rather than possessing it by nature.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines content as satisfied and quiet in mind; raiment as clothing; a state as a condition of being; poverty as want of property; and convenient as suitable and fit.
webster_full: CONTENT, a. Rest or quietness of the mind in the present condition; satisfaction such as to stop opposition or complaint.
RAIMENT, n. Clothing in general; vestments; vesture; garments.
STATE, n. Condition; the circumstances of a being or thing at any given time; situation; rank.
POVERTY, n. Destitution of property; indigence; want of convenient means of subsistence.
CONVENIENT, a. Fit; suitable; proper; commodious; affording ease; adapted to use or to wants.
corruption_summary: Yorkshire Cistercian house that moved five times in forty-three years before building at Byland in 1177, with its great west rose window.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is contentment, which the New Testament sets at a very low material threshold: “And having food and raiment let us be therewith content” (1Ti 6:8). Paul is careful to present it as an acquired discipline and not a disposition, “for I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content” (Phi 4:11), which is a comfort to anyone who has not managed it yet.

The live temptation for a homeless community is to make a grievance of the homelessness or a merit of it, and Byland did neither; it kept the offices and kept moving. Agur's prayer asks for the middle condition on explicitly spiritual grounds: “give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with food convenient for me” (Pro 30:8). The Psalm prescribes the posture for a people with no settled ground: “Trust in the LORD, and do good; so shalt thou dwell in the land, and verily thou shalt be fed” (Psa 37:3). Forty-three years later they had a rose window.

pos: n. (the Cistercian abbey founded from Fountains in 1152, now a ruin in a public park in the middle of Leeds)
etymology: From Old Norse kirkja, a church, with Old English stall, a place or site; the church site.
biblical_def: Kirkstall Abbey was founded in 1152 when Henry de Lacy gave the Aire valley site to a colony from Fountains, and it was built quickly and almost entirely in one campaign, which is why it is the most coherent Cistercian plan left in England; most of the church walls and the chapter house stand. It grew wool and ran iron forges, declined after the Black Death, and was dissolved in 1539. Leeds then grew out to meet it: the abbey now sits in a public park between a main road and the river, in the middle of a manufacturing city, with a museum in its gatehouse. The dictionary records Kirkstall for that setting, which is a parable nobody arranged. A house built in an empty valley to be away from the world ended with the world built around it, and Christ's metaphors for his people are not withdrawal but salt and light, both of which only work in contact: salt that has lost its savour is good for nothing, and a light is set up in order to be seen and to make God glorified.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines salt as a substance used to season and preserve; savour as taste and flavour; to shine as to emit light; to glorify as to honour; and darkness as absence of light.
webster_full: SALT, n. Common salt, used to season food and to preserve meats from putrefaction; taste; smack; savor.
SAVOR, n. Taste or odor; something that perceptibly affects the organs of taste and smell; flavor.
SHINE, v.i. To emit rays of light; to give light; to be bright; to be lively and animated.
GLORIFY, v.t. To praise; to magnify and honor in worship; to make glorious; to exalt to glory.
DARKNESS, n. Absence of light; obscurity; a state of being intellectually clouded; wickedness.
corruption_summary: Cistercian abbey founded from Fountains in 1152 in an empty Aire valley, now a ruin in a public park in the middle of Leeds.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Christ's figures for his people both require contact with what they act upon. Salt is useless once it is only itself: “if the salt have lost his savour, wherewith shall it be salted? it is thenceforth good for nothing” (Mat 5:13). Light exists to be looked at and to redirect attention: “Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven” (Mat 5:16).

The live temptation is the one the Cistercians institutionalised, a holiness measured by distance, and the irony of Kirkstall is that a city came and settled around the retreat. Isaiah's promise is about light arriving where people already are: “The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light” (Isa 9:2). And Paul locates the illumination inside believers, for the purpose of being carried out of them: God “hath shined in our hearts, to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2Co 4:6). A park full of people round a ruined church is not a defeat.

pos: n. (the Devon abbey founded about 974, which had a printing press by 1525, among the earliest in any English monastery)
etymology: Old English Tefingstoc, the settlement on the Tavy, a British river name, with stoc, a place.
biblical_def: Tavistock Abbey on the western edge of Dartmoor was founded about 974 by Ordgar, Earl of Devon, burned by Danes in 997, rebuilt, and grew rich on the Devon tin trade, of which it held the stannary court. Its distinction is a printing press. By 1525 the abbey had one, probably the earliest in an English religious house, and a monk named Thomas Rychard printed on it a translation of Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy into English and then the Statutes of the Stannaries, a legal text for tinners, with a Cornish version; four Tavistock books are known. The abbey was dissolved in 1539 and almost nothing of it remains above ground. The dictionary records Tavistock for the press, which was in the right hands for four years and went to the right sort of work: a book of consolation and a book of law, both in the languages people actually used. Scripture orders the writing to be plain so that a man may read it running, and it commands the training of children in the way they should go.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a press as a machine for printing; plain as clear and evident; to train as to educate and discipline; nurture as instruction and food; and admonition as gentle reproof.
webster_full: PRESS, n. An instrument or machine by which any body is squeezed; a printing press; the art or business of printing.
PLAIN, a. Evident to the understanding; clear; manifest; not obscure; open; artless; sincere.
TRAIN, v.t. To draw along; to educate; to teach and form by practice; to discipline; to break and accustom.
NURTURE, n. That which nourishes; food; diet; education; instruction; the act of bringing up.
ADMONITION, n. Gentle reproof; counseling against fault or error; instruction in duties; caution.
corruption_summary: Devon abbey of about 974, holder of the stannary court, which ran a printing press by 1525 and printed Boethius in English and the Stannary statutes.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that plain writing is a commanded form of service. The LORD tells Habakkuk how to publish what he has been given: “Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it” (Hab 2:2). A press in a monastery turning out a legal text for tinners in their own language was doing that, and so was the English Boethius.

The live temptation with a new technology is to reserve it for the learned, which is exactly what most of the early church presses did and what Tavistock's did not. Scripture places the first duty of teaching in the home and in the plainest possible terms: “Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it” (Pro 22:6), with the manner specified as well as the matter, “bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord” (Eph 6:4). And the effect of the text itself is promised to the least educated reader: “it giveth understanding unto the simple” (Psa 119:130).

pos: n. (the Dorset nunnery founded by Alfred for his daughter, the richest house of women in England)
etymology: Old English Sceaftesburh, perhaps the fortress of the shaft or on the ridge, with burh, a fortified place.
biblical_def: Shaftesbury Abbey was founded about 888 by Alfred the Great on a Dorset hilltop, with his daughter Ethelgiva as its first abbess, and it became the wealthiest house of women in England. The body of Edward the Martyr, murdered at Corfe in 978, was brought there and the abbey became a pilgrimage resort on that account; Canute died at Shaftesbury. Its abbess held land across four counties, sat as a baron would in all but name, and the saying ran that if the abbot of Glastonbury could marry the abbess of Shaftesbury their heir would hold more land than the king. It was dissolved in 1539 and demolished; only foundations remain in a garden. The dictionary records Shaftesbury for the women. Whatever is to be said against the system of vows, the houses of women in England sheltered widows, taught girls, copied books and fed the poor for eight hundred years, and Scripture has a settled vocabulary for such a life: the widow indeed continuing in supplications night and day, Anna in the temple, and Dorcas full of good works and almsdeeds.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a widow as a woman who has lost her husband; desolate as destitute and forsaken; supplication as humble entreaty; almsdeeds as acts of charity; and godliness as piety toward God.
webster_full: WIDOW, n. A woman who has lost her husband by death; a woman bereaved of a husband.
DESOLATE, a. Destitute of inhabitants; forsaken of friends; left alone; afflicted; comfortless.
SUPPLICATION, n. Entreaty; humble and earnest prayer in worship; petition; the act of imploring.
ALMSDEED, n. An act of charity; a charitable gift or deed done for the relief of the poor.
GODLINESS, n. Piety; belief in God, with reverence and obedience; a religious life.
corruption_summary: Dorset nunnery founded by Alfred about 888 for his daughter Ethelgiva, the richest house of women in England, dissolved in 1539 and demolished.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture honours a particular kind of woman's life without inventing an order for it. Paul describes her exactly: “she that is a widow indeed, and desolate, trusteth in God, and continueth in supplications and prayers night and day” (1Ti 5:5). Luke shows the thing done, in Anna, “which departed not from the temple, but served God with fastings and prayers night and day” (Luk 2:37).

The live temptation at a great abbey of women was the one that attended all such wealth, an abbess who was in practice a baron and a shrine that drew pilgrims and their money. The pattern Scripture actually praises is a working one: Dorcas at Joppa “was full of good works and almsdeeds which she did” (Act 9:36), and Paul specifies the adornment that belongs to women professing godliness, “with good works” (1Ti 2:10). Shaftesbury fed the poor of four counties, which is the part of its record the Dissolution did not replace.

pos: n. (the Hampshire nunnery whose abbey church the townspeople bought for a hundred pounds in 1544)
etymology: Old English Rumesig, Rum's island, a dry rise in the Test valley marsh.
biblical_def: Romsey Abbey in the Test valley was founded about 907 by Edward the Elder as a house of nuns and refounded under the Benedictine rule in 967, and it educated the daughters of the Anglo-Saxon and then the Norman nobility; Matilda, who married Henry I, was brought up there, and her claim that she had never taken vows was argued before Anselm. The abbey church was rebuilt from about 1120 on a scale out of all proportion to the town, and it holds two early crucifixion carvings, one an eleventh-century rood of great severity on the exterior wall. At the Dissolution the nuns were pensioned and the church was sold to the townspeople for a hundred pounds in 1544; the bill of sale is kept in the church. The dictionary records Romsey for the women it taught and for the plain standard by which Scripture measures a woman's life. Proverbs sets the hand stretched out to the poor beside the fear of the LORD and dismisses what the world grades by: favour is deceitful and beauty is vain.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines favour as kind regard; deceitful as tending to mislead; beauty as an assemblage of graces pleasing the eye; to stretch out as to extend; and holy as set apart to sacred use.
webster_full: FAVOR, n. Kind regard; kindness; countenance; propitious aspect; a kind act or office; leave; good will.
DECEITFUL, a. Tending to mislead, deceive or ensnare; fraudulent; full of deceit; delusive.
BEAUTY, n. An assemblage of graces, or an assemblage of properties in the form of the person or any other object, which pleases the eye.
STRETCH, v.t. To extend; to reach forth; to spread; to draw out in length or breadth.
HOLY, a. Properly, whole, entire or perfect, in a moral sense; hence, pure in heart; set apart to a sacred use.
corruption_summary: Hampshire nunnery of about 907, a school for noblewomen including the future Queen Matilda, whose church the town bought for a hundred pounds in 1544.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the measure Scripture uses for a woman's life, and it is a hand and a fear rather than a face. Proverbs puts the charity first: “She stretcheth out her hand to the poor; yea, she reacheth forth her hands to the needy” (Pro 31:20), and then dismisses what the world grades by, “Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised” (Pro 31:30).

The live temptation at a nunnery that educated heiresses was to become an instrument of family strategy, with girls placed in it and vows claimed or denied as a marriage required, which is precisely what Matilda's case before Anselm turned on. Paul describes the single life as a genuine freedom for the Lord's things, “The unmarried woman careth for the things of the Lord, that she may be holy both in body and in spirit” (1Co 7:34), and he never makes it a higher state, since “Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled” (Heb 13:4). A vow extracted from a child is neither.

pos: n. (the Derbyshire double monastery and Mercian royal burial place, where Guthlac took the tonsure and the Danes wintered in 873)
etymology: Old English Hrypadun, the hill of the Hrype people, a tribal name also found in Ripon.
biblical_def: Repton on the Trent in Derbyshire was the chief church of Mercia in the seventh and eighth centuries, a double monastery of men and women under an abbess, where the Mercian kings were buried in a crypt that still stands under the parish church, with its spiral columns and vaulted roof among the finest Anglo-Saxon work in England. Guthlac took the tonsure at Repton before going out to the fens. In 873 the Danish Great Army wintered there, destroyed the monastery, dug a ditch using the church as a gatehouse, and buried a great many of their dead in a mound nearby. The monastery was never rebuilt; a priory came later, and the school occupies its gatehouse. The dictionary records Repton for the renunciations made in it. Guthlac gave up a war band and an inheritance, and the Mercian princesses who ruled the house gave up marriages; Scripture does not treat such renunciation as meritorious but it does treat it as real, and Christ's own terms are uncompromising about what following him costs.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to forsake as to quit entirely; perfect as finished and complete; treasure as accumulated wealth; a disciple as a learner and follower; and to follow as to go after.
webster_full: FORSAKE, v.t. To quit or leave entirely; to desert; to abandon; to depart from; to renounce.
PERFECT, a. Finished; complete; consummate; not defective; having all that is requisite to its nature and kind.
TREASURE, n. Wealth accumulated; a store or stock of money in reserve; something very much valued.
DISCIPLE, n. A learner; a scholar; one who receives or professes to receive instruction from another.
FOLLOW, v.t. To go after or behind; to attend; to accompany; to pursue; to imitate; to obey.
corruption_summary: Derbyshire double monastery and Mercian royal burial place, with a surviving Anglo-Saxon crypt; destroyed when the Danish Great Army wintered there in 873.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Christ's terms for discipleship are severe and are addressed to everyone rather than to a professional class. He says to one rich man, “If thou wilt be perfect, go and sell that thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven” (Mat 19:21), and he states the general rule in the crowd's hearing: “whosoever he be of you that forsaketh not all that he hath, he cannot be my disciple” (Luk 14:33).

The live temptation is the medieval settlement, in which renunciation was contracted out to monks and nuns while everyone else was excused, and both halves of that arrangement are errors. Christ's warning about possessions is given to a man in a crowd, not to a novice: “a man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth” (Luk 12:15). And the alternative he offers is not poverty for its own sake but a transfer, “lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven” (Mat 6:20). Guthlac gave up a war band; the Danes who destroyed his house were accumulating.

pos: n. (the Lincolnshire abbey that received the relics of Oswald, and whose abbot was the Mercian king Ethelred)
etymology: Old English Beardaneg, Bearda's island, a rise in the Witham marsh.
biblical_def: Bardney Abbey stood on a rise above the Witham in Lindsey, founded in the late seventh century and famous in Bede for two things. Ethelred, king of Mercia, abdicated in 704, became a monk at Bardney and then its abbot, and died there. And when the bones of Oswald of Northumbria were brought to Bardney by his niece Osthryth, the monks refused them entry because Oswald had ruled over them as a conqueror, and left the wagon outside all night, whereupon a pillar of light is said to have stood over it until morning, after which they took the relics in gladly and the house became a shrine. The abbey was destroyed by the Danes, refounded as a Benedictine priory in 1087, and dissolved in 1538. The dictionary records Bardney for the second story, which is a case study in how a cult begins. A sign resolved a political grudge and produced a shrine, and Scripture's standing warning is about worship that rests on human precept: a fear toward God taught by the commandments of men, and in vain.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a precept as a command and rule; a commandment as an order given by authority; in vain as to no purpose; an idol as an image worshipped; and tradition as doctrine orally delivered.
webster_full: PRECEPT, n. Any commandment or order intended as an authoritative rule of action; a maxim; a rule of conduct.
COMMANDMENT, n. A command; a mandate; an order or injunction given by authority; a precept.
VAIN, a. Empty; worthless; having no substance, value or importance; ineffectual; fruitless.
IDOL, n. An image, form or representation, consecrated as an object of worship; a person or thing greatly loved.
TRADITION, n. The delivery of opinions, doctrines, practices and rites from ancestors to posterity; oral delivery.
corruption_summary: Lincolnshire abbey whose abbot was the abdicated Mercian king Ethelred, and which refused Oswald's relics until a pillar of light appeared over the wagon.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the test Isaiah applies to a devout-looking people, which is whether their reverence came from God or from custom: “this people draw near me with their mouth, and with their lips do honour me, but have removed their heart far from me” (Isa 29:13). Christ quotes it at the Pharisees and draws the conclusion: “in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men” (Mat 15:9).

The live temptation is the shrine, and Bardney shows the mechanism with unusual clarity: a political refusal, a wonder, a reversal, and then a cult with offerings. The Psalter states the law of such devotion, that worshippers come to resemble what they venerate: “They that make them are like unto them; so is every one that trusteth in them” (Psa 115:8). Paul's test for any inherited practice is whether it is of Christ or of men: beware of being spoiled “after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ” (Col 2:8). A king who became an abbot is the better half of Bardney's story.

pos: n. (the Essex nunnery founded about 666, the greatest house of women in England, whose abbess held baronial rank)
etymology: Old English Berecingum, the settlement of Bereca's people, on the Roding near the Thames.
biblical_def: Barking Abbey in Essex was founded about 666 by Erkenwald, bishop of London, for his sister Ethelburga, and from the tenth century refoundation to the Dissolution it was the premier house of women in England. Its abbess was appointed by the crown, held the manor and its courts, and ranked as a baron in all but the writ; three queens and two royal daughters were among its abbesses. Clemence of Barking, a nun there in the twelfth century, translated the life of St Catherine into Anglo-Norman verse and is one of the earliest named women writers in England. The abbey surrendered in 1539 and was pulled down to the ground; only the Curfew Tower stands. The dictionary records Barking for the question of jurisdiction that such a house forced. An abbess appointed by a king, holding land of a king, exercising courts in a king's name, had to answer eventually where the line between the two authorities ran, and the New Testament's answer is Christ's own division of the coin and the apostles' refusal in the council: we ought to obey God rather than men.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to render as to give back and pay; Caesar as the title of the Roman emperors; to hearken as to listen and obey; to judge as to decide; and to obey as to comply with a command.
webster_full: RENDER, v.t. To return; to pay back; to give in return; to give on demand what is due.
CAESAR, n. A title of the Roman emperors; hence used for the civil power or supreme magistrate.
HEARKEN, v.i. To listen; to lend the ear; to attend to what is uttered, with eagerness or curiosity; to obey.
JUDGE, v.t. To hear and determine, as in causes on trial; to decide; to form an opinion; to try.
OBEY, v.t. To comply with the commands, orders or instructions of a superior; to be ruled by; to submit to.
corruption_summary: Essex nunnery founded about 666 for Ethelburga, premier house of women in England, whose crown-appointed abbess held baronial rank; demolished after 1539.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the division Christ made with a coin in his hand, which gives the civil power a real claim and a limited one: “Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's” (Mat 22:21). The apostles apply it when the council forbids them to preach, and they put the decision to the council itself: “Whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye” (Act 4:19).

The live temptation when church office carries civil power is that the two claims stop being distinguishable, and an abbess who held courts for the crown was in no position to tell them apart. The apostles' own ground is not a theory of jurisdiction but a necessity: “For we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard” (Act 4:20), and when pressed again they answer in five words that settle the order of obedience, “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29). Barking was dissolved by the same crown that had appointed its abbesses.

pos: n. (the Wiltshire nunnery of the West Saxon kings, home of Edith, dissolved in 1539 and granted to the Herberts)
etymology: Old English Wiltun, the farm on the river Wylye, which also gives Wiltshire its name.
biblical_def: Wilton Abbey, two miles from Salisbury, was a house of nuns of West Saxon royal foundation, enlarged by Alfred and richly endowed by Edgar, whose daughter Edith lived and died there and became its saint; Goscelin wrote her life, and Edith is said to have refused the abbacies offered her and preferred to serve in the house. Wilton educated royal and noble women for six centuries; Queen Edith, wife of the Confessor, rebuilt its church in stone. It was dissolved in 1539 and the site was granted to William Herbert, who pulled the abbey down and built Wilton House out of it; his descendants hold it still. The dictionary records Wilton because the Dissolution is the plainest case in English history of property taken by power, and Scripture names that sin directly: men covet fields and take them by violence, and houses, and take them away. The question put to the religious at such a moment is Daniel's, and the three men in Babylon had the only answer that holds when deliverance is not promised: our God is able to deliver us, but if not, we will not serve thy gods.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to covet as to desire inordinately; violence as physical force unlawfully exercised; to oppress as to burden unjustly; to confess as to own and acknowledge; and able as having power.
webster_full: COVET, v.t. To desire inordinately; to desire that which it is unlawful to obtain or possess; to long for.
VIOLENCE, n. Physical force; strength of action or motion; unjust force; outrage; injury done to rights or property.
OPPRESS, v.t. To load or burden with unreasonable impositions; to treat with unjust severity or hardship.
CONFESS, v.t. To own, acknowledge or avow, as a crime, a fault or a debt; to acknowledge faith in Christ.
ABLE, a. Having physical power sufficient; having competent power or means; having strength or skill.
corruption_summary: Wiltshire nunnery of West Saxon royal foundation, home of Edith, dissolved in 1539 and granted to William Herbert, who built Wilton House from its stones.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the seizure of property by those with power is a sin Scripture names without euphemism. Micah describes it in its ordinary form: “And they covet fields, and take them by violence; and houses, and take them away: so they oppress a man and his house” (Mic 2:2). Whatever is to be said about the state of the monasteries, that verse describes what happened to Wilton and to several hundred houses besides.

The live temptation when the state turns on the church is to bargain, and the only answer that holds is the one given in Babylon with the furnace already heated. The three men assert God's power first, “our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace” (Dan 3:17), and then remove the condition that would make their obedience a wager: “But if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods” (Dan 3:18). Christ attaches his own acknowledgment to that kind of confession: “Whosoever therefore shall confess me before men, him will I confess also before my Father which is in heaven” (Mat 10:32).
